lesson_title: Four Thousand People Can Be Wrong
hook_text: A radio poll of 4 000 people says 78 percent want matric exams scrapped. A survey of 1 000 says 41 percent. The smaller one is right. Here is why.
clip_script: A radio station asks listeners to SMS yes or no: should matric exams be scrapped? Four thousand people reply and 78 percent say yes. Big number, must be true? Ask who replied. Only listeners of that one station. Only the ones who cared enough to pay for an SMS. Four thousand out of maybe 850 000 listeners. The sample picked itself, and people who pick themselves are the ones with the strongest feelings. That is lean, a tilt built into the method, and a bigger sample does not fix lean; it just gives you more of the same tilt. Meanwhile researchers chose 1 000 adults across the country, fairly, and found 41 percent. Smaller and fair beats bigger and tilted. Same at the tuck shop: the owner asks at the counter and 45 of 50 are happy; an anonymous form says 28 of 50. So before you believe a number, ask three things: who asked, who answered, and how they asked. Say it: bigger does not fix the lean.
visual_style: A radio with 4 000 tiny SMS bubbles pouring out, all from one corner of a map; a second map with 1 000 dots spread evenly; a tilted bar labelled lean that stays tilted as it grows; the tuck shop counter with 45 nodding heads and an anonymous box with 28.
pacing: The poll fast, the who-replied questions in a rhythm, the lean idea with a beat, the tuck shop fast, the three questions slow.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson for random error against bias, slipped digits, the wrong average and auditing a report.
